wine.name: Krug Grande Cuvée
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier, in proportions that change with each Édition.
wine.sites: Plots across the villages of Champagne, each kept apart as its own wine, and a library of reserve wines from many years.
wine.making: Each plot is fermented on its own in small, old oak casks rather than steel, so that every wine can be judged apart before blending. More than a hundred and twenty wines from more than ten years are blended, reserve wines among them, and the bottles rest about seven years on their lees in the Reims cellars.
wine.glass: Toasted brioche, roasted hazelnut and candied lemon peel over ripe pear and honeyed pastry, with a fine, persistent mousse, a broad, almost vinous weight and a long, dry, faintly smoky finish.
wine.ageing: Drinks well on release and keeps developing for a decade or two after it, gaining toffee, coffee and dried fig.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass shows it better than a narrow flute.

label.means: The release's place in the line of yearly blends; each Édition is built around one harvest.
A code on the back label that opens, on the house's site, the story of that bottle.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.

records.table: Krug Grande Cuvée is the house's whole idea in one bottle: more than a hundred and twenty wines from over ten years, fermented in small old casks and aged about seven years. It drinks like a mature white Burgundy with bubbles, so pour it in a wine glass.
records.story: Joseph Krug (1800 to 1866), born in Mainz, learned Champagne at the house of Jacquesson before founding his own in Reims in 1843. In 1848, as the house tells it, he set down his creed in a personal notebook: to make the fullest expression of Champagne every year, whatever the weather, by blending the wines of many plots and many years. His son took over at his death in 1866, the year the house moved to the Rue Coquebert in Reims. Until 1978 the blend was sold as Private Cuvée; that year the house renamed it Grande Cuvée. Beside it the house made vintage wines, and in the 1970s it added a rosé and, from the walled Clos du Mesnil bought in 1971, a Chardonnay of one vineyard first made from the 1979 vintage, but the blend remained the house's purpose. Krug kept fermenting in small oak casks while most houses turned to steel tanks, and it built a library of reserve wines from many years for the cellar master to draw on. In the 2010s the house began to print an Édition number on the front label, so that a guest can tell one year's Grande Cuvée from the next and read the harvest it was built around. A sommelier sells it as a wine to be tasted, not a toast to be drunk.

others.name: Krug Vintage
others.note: Declared years only, made with the same small casks and long cellar ageing as the Grande Cuvée.

others.name: Krug Clos du Mesnil
others.note: Chardonnay alone from one walled vineyard in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, first made from the 1979 vintage.

others.name: Krug Clos d'Ambonnay
others.note: The Pinot Noir counterpart from a tiny walled plot in Ambonnay, first made in 1995.

traps: Grande Cuvée carries no vintage, yet it spends longer in the cellar than many vintage Champagnes.
Clos du Mesnil is Chardonnay from Le Mesnil-sur-Oger; Clos d'Ambonnay is Pinot Noir from Ambonnay.
An Édition number counts the yearly creations of the blend; it is not a vintage year.

cards.back: The wine of every plot, kept apart so that each can be judged on its own before blending; the casks are old ones, not new oak.

questions.exp: Grande Cuvée is a multi vintage blend of well over a hundred wines, reserve wines among them; a single vintage would carry its year, and Clos du Mesnil is a separate Chardonnay.

report: Recheck of 12 November 2026: every fact beyond the Codex was searched; the record now rests on Krug's own pages for its dates and methods and on two secondary sources for the rest, with the full list in reviews/recheck-champagne.json.
Private Cuvée is said by one guide (Fine and Rare, mirrored by Vinfolio) to date from 1862; with no independent second source the story says only that the blend was sold under that name until 1978.
The first Édition printed on the label is the 163rd in two accounts (Quill and Pad, Openers); the year the numbering was first disclosed is not settled, so the story says the 2010s.

changed: making, table: the bottles rest about seven years on their lees, as the house's own Édition notes say, where the record said at least seven; the casks are said to be old rather than to let the wine breathe without any taste of wood, a claim no source gave.

story: the Private Cuvée was sold under that name until 1978, where the record said for more than a century, a span resting on one guide; Joseph Krug's son took over in 1866, the year of the move to the Rue Coquebert (Wikipedia and the house's Japanese importer).

story: the house made vintage wines before it added a rosé in the 1970s (1976 by its own account) and the Clos du Mesnil, now said to be bought in 1971, as Krug's own Individuality page says; the record had the vintage added after 1978.
story and cards[1]: the Édition number is printed on the front label from the 163rd Édition, in the 2010s, where the record said numbered since 2016, a year no source gave.
cards[0]: the back now says why each plot is kept apart, to be judged before blending, as the house tells it, in place of the unsourced breathing casks.
questions[1].exp: no longer claims where Jacquesson stood in 1843; it teaches the 1866 move to the Rue Coquebert instead.

sources: the Patience page and the krug.com address of the old Our Story page were never found in a search and are replaced by pages the search returned (Our Story, Individuality, the 172nd Édition notes, Vinepair).

wine.name: Dom Pérignon
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, in close to equal parts that shift with the year.
wine.sites: Chiefly Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs, the Montagne de Reims and Aÿ, with fruit from the abbey's own Premier Cru vineyard at Hautvillers.
wine.making: Made only in declared vintages. Since the vintages after 1964 its base wines have been fermented in stainless steel with no oak. The wine then ages on its lees for the better part of a decade before the first release, and the same vintage returns later as Plénitude 2 after far longer on its lees.
wine.glass: Toasted almond, white peach and fresh brioche, with a smoky note of struck flint and a fine, creamy mousse; with age it moves towards roasted coffee, candied ginger and acacia honey.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it gains depth for fifteen to twenty years and more, which is why the house releases each vintage again as Plénitudes.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: Dom Pérignon is always the wine of one year, and the label prints it.
The second Plénitude: the same vintage released again after far longer on its lees.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.

records.table: Dom Pérignon is Moët & Chandon's prestige cuvée, named for the Benedictine monk who kept the cellars of Hautvillers. It is always a single vintage of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, aged for years on its lees before release.
records.story: An Épernay wine merchant of the Moët family founded the house in 1743, and his grandson Jean-Rémy Moët (1758 to 1841) carried its wines across Europe; the Emperor Napoleon (1769 to 1821) visited him at Épernay and awarded him the Légion d'honneur. In 1833 the house passed to Jean-Rémy's son and his son-in-law, a Chandon, and took the name Moët & Chandon. Its prestige cuvée honours Dom Pierre Pérignon, cellarer of the Benedictine abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 until his death in 1715. He did not invent sparkling Champagne, a tale first told in 1821, long after his death: he blended grapes from different vineyards and, by most accounts, refined the making of white wine from black grapes, while the wines his abbey sold did not sparkle. The name Dom Pérignon belonged to the house of Mercier, which passed it to Moët after a marriage between the two families in 1927. The first Dom Pérignon, from the 1921 vintage, was released in 1936. It has since been made only in declared years, and the house releases the same vintage a second and a third time, as Plénitudes, after far longer ageing on the lees.

others.name: Moët Impérial
others.note: The house's non vintage Brut of Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay, its everyday style.

others.name: Moët & Chandon Grand Vintage
others.note: The vintage wine under the Moët name, made apart from Dom Pérignon.

others.name: Dom Pérignon Rosé
others.note: The rosé of a declared year, made in far smaller quantity.

traps: Dom Pérignon did not invent sparkling Champagne: he blended grapes from many vineyards, and the tale of his bubbles was first told in 1821.
Dom Pérignon is always vintage dated; Moët Impérial is the house's non vintage Brut.
P2 is not a different blend: it is the same vintage disgorged after a far longer stay on its lees.

cards.front: Moët & Chandon names its prestige cuvée for a monk. Who was he, and what did he truly do?
cards.back: Dom Pierre Pérignon, cellarer of the abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 to his death in 1715; he blended grapes from many vineyards, but he did not invent the bubbles.

cards.front: Moët & Chandon's Dom Pérignon: which grapes, and is there a non vintage version?
cards.back: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in close to equal parts; it is always the wine of a single declared year.

questions.exp: Dom Pérignon blends Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in close to equal parts in each declared year; Meunier goes into Moët Impérial, the house's non vintage Brut.

opts: The house of Mercier passed it on after a family marriage
The abbey of Hautvillers sold it at auction

The Comité Champagne granted it to the house
questions.exp: The name was an unused mark of the house of Mercier, given to Moët after a Mercier married a Chandon in 1927; the 1921 vintage was the first released.

wine.name: Cristal
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, in shares that change with the year.
wine.sites: Only the house's own Grand Cru vineyards: Verzenay, Verzy and Beaumont-sur-Vesle on the Montagne de Reims, Aÿ in the Marne valley, and Avize, Cramant and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger in the Côte des Blancs.
wine.making: Made only in years the house judges ripe enough, from estate parcels vinified apart, a share of them in oak casks, with the malolactic conversion usually blocked to keep its tension. It rests about six years in the cellars and eight months more after disgorging.
wine.glass: Meyer lemon, white peach and fresh almond over crushed chalk, with a delicate, creamy mousse; time brings toasted brioche, hazelnut and honeyed pastry while the line stays taut and saline.
wine.ageing: Taut on release, it opens after eight to ten years and keeps for twenty or more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass, the cellophane left on until the bottle is opened.

label.means: The cuvée's name, from the clear glass of the first bottles made for the Tsar.
The house that makes it; Cristal is its prestige cuvée, not a separate producer.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.

records.table: Cristal, Louis Roederer's prestige cuvée, was first made in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II, in the clear bottle he asked for. It comes only from the house's own Grand Cru vines, Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, and only in years ripe enough.
records.story: Cristal takes its name from glass. The house that became Louis Roederer was a Reims wine business recorded in 1776. A nephew of its owner inherited it in 1833 and gave it his own name, Louis Roederer, and under him and his son the house sold widely in Russia. In 1876 Tsar Alexander II (1818 to 1881) asked the house to set aside a cuvée for his court each year, and it was bottled in clear glass with a flat base so that, as the story is told, nothing could be hidden in the bottle or its punt. The revolution of 1917 ended the imperial orders and much of the house's Russian trade, and Cristal later became a wine any guest could order; a rosé followed with the 1974 harvest. Unlike most houses, Roederer built its prestige wine on its own vineyards rather than on bought grapes, and Cristal has been made only in the years the house judges ripe enough. The coloured cellophane round each bottle is there to keep light from a wine in clear glass.

others.name: Cristal Rosé
others.note: The rosé of a declared year, first made in 1974, in far smaller quantity.

others.note: The house's numbered multi vintage Brut, which replaced Brut Premier.

others.name: Louis Roederer Blanc de Blancs

Cristal is Louis Roederer's cuvée from Reims, not the wine of Roederer Estate in California.
The clear bottle dates from the Tsar's order of 1876; the cellophane wrap is there to keep the light out.

cards.front: Louis Roederer Cristal: for whom was it first made, and when?
cards.back: For Tsar Alexander II of Russia, in 1876, in a clear glass bottle with a flat base.

wine.name: La Grande Année
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir, from about three fifths to two thirds, with Chardonnay for the rest.
wine.sites: About twenty Grand and Premier Cru villages, the Pinot Noir chiefly from Aÿ and Verzenay, the Chardonnay largely from Chouilly.
wine.making: Every base wine is fermented in oak barrels, old ones and never new. The wine is then aged under natural cork rather than a crown cap, on its lees for more than twice the three years the appellation asks of a vintage, and every bottle is riddled and disgorged by hand.
wine.glass: Baked apple, ripe pear and roasted hazelnut over toasted brioche, with a savoury, almost mushroom depth from the Pinot Noir and the barrels, a firm, vinous body and a fine, steady mousse.
wine.ageing: Rich enough on release, it grows more savoury and nutty over ten to twenty years.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a few minutes in the glass help; a tulip or a white wine glass.

label.means: The great year: Bollinger's name for its vintage wine, made only in years the house declares.
The appellation, which requires a vintage wine to rest at least three years before release.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.

records.table: La Grande Année is Bollinger's vintage Champagne: Pinot Noir led, fermented entirely in oak barrels and aged under cork for years before it is disgorged by hand. It has the weight to stand beside a main course.
records.story: Elisabeth Bollinger, known as Lily (1899 to 1977), cycled through the vineyards of Aÿ to inspect them, and after her husband's death in 1941 she ran the house through the German occupation and on until 1971. The house she led had been founded at Aÿ in 1829 by three partners, one of them a young German from Württemberg whose name the house carries, and it received a Royal Warrant from Queen Victoria (1819 to 1901) in 1884. Lily released R.D. in 1967, a 1952 vintage disgorged late after a long rest on its lees, and in 1969 made the first Vieilles Vignes Françaises. The house kept old ways that others dropped: fermenting in old barrels, holding part of its reserve wines in magnum under cork and tending two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir inside Aÿ, the source of Vieilles Vignes Françaises. La Grande Année is the wine in which all of that shows: a vintage of Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, fermented in barrel, aged under cork for years and riddled by hand, and made only in the years the house declares.

others.name: Bollinger Special Cuvée
others.note: The non vintage Brut, Pinot Noir led, with part of its reserve wines kept in magnum.

others.name: Bollinger R.D.
others.note: La Grande Année held far longer on its lees and disgorged late; R.D. means recently disgorged.

others.name: Bollinger Vieilles Vignes Françaises
others.note: A Blanc de Noirs from two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir in Aÿ, first made in 1969.

traps: R.D. is not a vineyard or a separate blend: it is La Grande Année disgorged years later.
Vieilles Vignes Françaises is ungrafted Pinot Noir, not old vine Chardonnay.
La Grande Année is fermented in oak, yet it is not meant to taste of new wood: the barrels are old.

cards.front: Bollinger La Grande Année: how is it fermented and aged?
cards.back: Entirely in old oak barrels, then aged under natural cork rather than a crown cap, and riddled and disgorged by hand.

cards.front: What does R.D. mean on a Bollinger label?
cards.back: Recently disgorged: La Grande Année left far longer on its lees and disgorged late, first released in 1967, in Lily Bollinger's time.

wine.name: Substance
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone: a Blanc de Blancs.
wine.sites: The domaine's own Grand Cru Chardonnay in Avize, in the Côte des Blancs.
wine.making: Each year's wine, fermented in barrels with native yeasts, is added to a solera begun in 1986 by most accounts, and a part of the whole is drawn off to bottle, so every bottle carries a little of every year since. It is bottled with little dosage after long lees ageing, and the label gives the date of disgorging.
wine.glass: Bruised apple, walnut and salted caramel with a note of fino Sherry, over crushed chalk and lemon peel; dry, broad and vinous, with a fine mousse and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, it gains nuttier, deeper notes for another decade, and many cellar it as they would white Burgundy.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, since colder it closes; decant it briefly if you like, or let it open in a white wine glass.

label.means: The grapes come from Avize, one of the seventeen Grand Cru villages of Champagne.
A white Champagne made from white grapes alone, here Chardonnay.
A grower making Champagne from its own grapes; printed as RM before the registration number.

records.table: Jacques Selosse is the Avize grower held up as the model for grower Champagne, and Substance is its Chardonnay drawn from a solera, as in a Sherry bodega. It tastes of walnut, bruised apple and chalk: pour it in a wine glass, a little warmer than most Champagne.
records.story: Jacques Selosse is a small domaine in Avize, in the Côte des Blancs, set up by its founder after the Second World War, in 1949 by several accounts. The family first made and bottled Champagne of its own in the years around 1960, rather than selling all its grapes to the houses. The founder's son, who had studied at the wine school in Beaune, joined him in 1974 and took charge in 1980. He brought Burgundy's ways back to Champagne: low yields, native yeasts, fermentation in barrels and a wine made first as a wine of place and only then as a sparkling wine. In 1986, by most accounts, he began a perpetual reserve of Avize Chardonnay on the model of a Sherry solera: each year the new wine goes into the reserve and a part of the whole is drawn off to bottle, so the blend carries a little of every year since it began. That wine is Substance. Its oxidative, nutty depth divided drinkers, but it made Selosse the model for the grower movement of the 1990s and 2000s, when small estates across Champagne began to bottle their own wines and to name their villages and plots on the label.

traps: Substance carries no vintage: it is drawn from a solera of many years.
Récoltant-Manipulant is a label code for a grower, not a mark of quality.
Its nutty, Sherry like notes come from age and air in the solera, not from any fortification.

cards.front: Jacques Selosse Substance: how is it made, and why does it carry no vintage?
cards.back: It is drawn from a solera of Avize Chardonnay begun in 1986 by most accounts: each year's wine is added and a part bottled, so every bottle blends many years.

cards.front: What did Jacques Selosse change in Champagne from 1980?
cards.back: It made Champagne as a wine of place, from low yields, native yeasts and barrels, and gave the grower movement its model.

questions.q: A guest is surprised that Selosse Substance shows no vintage. Which method explains it?
opts: A solera, topped up each year with new wine
A blend of declared vintages from bought grapes
Saignée, bleeding juice from the Pinot Noir vats
Carbon dioxide pumped into a Chardonnay before release
questions.exp: Substance is drawn from a solera of Avize Chardonnay begun in 1986 by most accounts; each year's wine refreshes it, so no single vintage applies. It uses no bought grapes and no saignée.

questions.q: Where did the heir who took charge of Jacques Selosse in 1980 train, before bringing barrel fermentation and low yields to Avize?
opts: Burgundy
Jerez
Bordeaux
Alsace
questions.exp: He studied in Burgundy, at the wine school in Beaune, and brought its handling of wine to Avize; Sherry gave only the idea of the solera behind Substance, not his training.

report: The domaine's founding is 1949 in several accounts and the 1950s in Wikipedia, so founded is left empty and the story says 1949 by several accounts.
The first own bottling is 1960 in Wikipedia, first trials in 1959 and the first Champagne sold in 1964 in another account; the story says the years around 1960.
The founder's son returned to the domaine in 1974 by most accounts and took charge in 1980 by Wikipedia and others; the story gives both.
The solera's start is 1986 in most accounts and 1987 in one; whether Substance comes from one parcel or two in Avize differs, so the record names the village only.

Recheck of 12 November 2026: the full source list is in reviews/recheck-champagne.json; the domaine keeps no site of its own that a search returned, so the primary source is the Comité Champagne for the label words.
